docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Legacy technologies that may still be around

In previous notes on information theory, we saw that there are particular components in the communications medium. A simplified version of this would show a transmitter, a channel, and a receiver.

From 1793, much of Europe was at war with France, and Ireland was occupied by England. A symptom of the wars between the English and French were recurring attempts by the French to use Ireland as a “back door” into England. It was clear from the French activity from 1796 to 1798 that the threat of invasion in Ireland by the French and their allies was real. The ease with which the French evaded the British fleet, the unprepared defense forces and fortifications and the possibility of indigenous support and revolution all lead to fears of invasion by the authorities.

Between 1804 and 1806 signal stations were established in a continuous line from Dublin, around the south coast and north to Malin Head. These facilitated (relatively!) rapid communications of orders and events to and from otherwise exposed and remote areas and followed similar developments in England and France.

Captain Sir William Augustus Smith was assistant engineer in the Lough Swilly district from 1798 until his death in 1831. The original sketches for the defensive works at Lough Swilly from Smith dating from 1799 are held at Trinity College, Dublin in two volumes. It can be hard to get access, and it is a “gloves only” operation.

At Lough Swilly, towers were constructed at Fanad Head and at Malin Head and their site, original construction and development are dated and well portrayed by the sketches of Sir William Smith.

Fig 1. A Donegal communications tower c. 1806.

Why the history lesson?

The title of this document is Legacy Communications. I can establish through primary sources that we had digital, semaphore-based communications operating at the speed of light from Donegal to Dublin from c. 1804, a Wide Area Network (WAN) using free-space optics!

Although the content of these notes are (c) John ORaw, I have requested permission to use, but I do not hold copyright to the image in Fig 1.

docs.title: 1. Technology Evolution
docs.text:
At time of writing, most of the world has access to ubiquitous, packet-based networking.

Original WAN technology was based on the ubiquitous network of its time, the telephone network.

In the late 1800s, data communications signals were analogue, and telephones were allocated a single channel per line for transmission. And before you ask, yes, we have electricity in Buncrana at that time as well. Do some background reading on the connection between the Swann family, the lightbulb, and early electrical generation.

Once the vacuum tube came along, more complex techniques became available such as frequency division multiplexing (FDM). Coaxial cables were used, and following military developments in World War II, microwave telecommunications emerged. From the 1960s, and with the development of pulse code modulation (PCM), digital telephony became feasible. Digital systems using Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) were developed, and multi-megabit communication links began to be installed, primarily using fiber optic networks.

The slightly tinny sound of a voice through the plain old telephone system (POTS) was the result of filters, restricting the voice signal to a bandpass of 300Hz-3.4KHz. Nyquist’s Theorem requires us to sample any analogue signal at twice the rate of its highest frequency component. If we assume a maximum frequency of 4 kHz, then our sampling frequency must be 8kHz. We can provide 256 discrete levels using eight bits, and in implementation, use compression algorithms to improve comprehensibility. 8-bit samples taken at 8 kHz results in a bit rate of 64 kb per second. This was the bandwidth used by design on all digital telephone systems and when telephone companies began to sell leased lines, they were sold in increments of 64 kb/s. In the mid-80's the most common digital hierarchy in use was Plesciosynchronous Digital Hierarchy (PDH). It is called 'plescio' (almost) because the transmission is neither wholly synchronous or asynchronous.

PDH, was superseded by Synchronous Digital hierarchy (SDH) and Synchronous Optical Networking (SONET), which took the PDH signals and multiplexed them into Synchronous Time-Division Multiplexing (STM).

The technologies I discuss in this section are a curiosity, you are unlikly to see them. However, understanding the underlying concepts and terminology is essential!

docs.title: 2. Terminology
docs.text:
Back in the last millennium, we had some clear demarcations on the scale of network connectivity and on the kind of technologies we used at each scale. Local Area Networks (LANs) normally spanned a single building or a campus (a group of buildings on the same contiguous site). Although there were many original technologies, Ethernet is now the dominant (and almost sole) technology in use. Modern LANs are expected to have high bandwidth (typically 10Gbps), low latency and very low bit/error rates.

Metropolitan Area Networks (MANs) were intended to span a large town of city, of the order of 10-20kms. Protocols were developed which worked on local cables or using line-of-sight microwave links. Original MAN technologies had bandwidths in Mbps, medium latency and medium bit/error rates. Wide Area Networks (WANs) had coverage of the rest of the country or the rest of the world. Many technologies were used, most of which were based on the old wide area network which existed, the old time-division multiplexing (TDM) telephony network. In TDM, each user is assigned to a time slot; no other station can send in that time slot. If a station has a lot of data to send, it can send only when its time slot comes up, even if all other time slots are empty. If a station has nothing to transmit when its time slot comes up, the time slot is sent empty and is wasted. Original WAN technologies had low bandwidths in Kbps or Mbps, high latency and medium bit/error rates.

Now, fiber optic cables have become ubiquitous both nationally and worldwide. Fibre Optics are characterized by low latency and almost unlimited bandwidth; Letterkenny IT currently has two external connections which are (theoretically!) capable of 1.6Tbs each. This is done by Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM), sending a single data stream at 10Gbps on one colour of light and allowing for up to 160 discrete colours. As fibre optic technology spread and carrier networks moved away from TDM, it became cheaper and more efficient to use LAN technologies to interconnect widely dispersed networks. In this document, we will briefly discuss the legacy technologies from TDM which you may occasionally come across for specific purposes. We will also discuss the current approaches to WAN connectivity.

There are a range of protocols which were developed, utilized, and deprecated over the last 30 years or so. I need to mention them because nothing in technology ever really goes away.

docs.title: 3. Topology
docs.text:
The connection from the customer to the network would need to run to the nearest telephone exchange and for that reason, has traditionally been called the last mile. To this day and regardless of the technology being used, we still call the final connection to the customer the local loop or last mile connection.

Fig 2. Last Mile.

The carrier needs a clear point of demarcation where their network ends and the customers network starts. This also demarks who is responsible to fix things, and where. A carrier or an Internet Service Provider (ISP) will install Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) as an active endpoint which they can test to. When we began designing WANs, the only available network was the TDM based telephony network. For technical reasons, this network was designed around 64 kbps channels and our original WAN technologies were the same.

docs.title: 4. Leased Lines
docs.text:
The phone network was designed for analogue signals and to use the same wires for data, we had to use modulators/de-modulators or modems. For domestic use, we had dial-up modems which shared phone lines. For WAN use, we had phone lines dedicated for modem use only. The carrier provided a modem as CPE with a phone connection outbound and a serial digital interface inbound; these were provided at both ends of a link. This was a point-to-point lease line. The advantage of this technology is that it used a fixed, always available 64kbps channel, dedicated entirely to the customer and the link. Because these links were dedicated, they were reliable and consistent, and we still see them used in critical infrastructures.

Typically, the carrier uses 2 or 4 wires for signaling and installs a modem at either end of the link. Once the signal gets to the exchange, it is sent on dedicated channels over the PDH/SDH network and out to the modem at the other side. These circuits are generally priced based on bandwidth required and distance between the two connected points. The downside of this network is that it permanently ties up lines, hardware, and channels and for this reason, is very expensive. The last 64kbps link we used in Donegal cost over €10,000 a year to operate, back when a house cost <€100k.

docs.title: 5. Circuit Switched Networks
docs.text:
As every link in a telephone network is brought up on demand as a point-to-point circuit, we refer to this as a circuit switched network. Switched circuits allow data connections that can be initiated when needed and terminated when communication is complete. This works much like a normal telephone line works for voice communication. Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) is a good example of circuit switching. When a router has data for a remote site, the switched circuit is initiated with the circuit number of the remote network. In the case of ISDN circuits, the device places a call to the telephone number of the remote ISDN circuit. When the two networks are connected and authenticated, they can transfer data. When the data transmission is complete, the call can be terminated.

An ISDN Basic rate connection allows for 2*64kbps channels and a 16-kbps channel for signaling.

There is also a primary rate ISDN. This is the equivalent of 32 channels of 64 kbps, with 30 channels usable for traffic and two channels utilized for signaling. This circuit has a total bit rate of 2.048 Mbps.

docs.title: 6. Packet Switched Networks
docs.text: Carrier packet switched networks were the pre-cursor of the modern Internet. Users share common carrier resources rather than having dedicated resources. Because this allows the carrier to make more efficient use of its infrastructure, the cost to the customer was generally much better than with point-to-point lines. In a packet switching setup, networks have connections into the carrier's network, and many customers share the carrier's network. The carrier can then create virtual circuits between customer’s sites by which packets of data are delivered from one to the other through the network.

docs.title: X.25
docs.text: In the early days of packet switched WANs, X. 25 networks were provided by carriers to allow for basic packet switched connections. Networks at the time were slow and unreliable and the protocol was built robustly to work in these conditions. In some niche industries like Aerospace, you may still see X.25.

docs.title: Frame Relay
docs.text:
Frame Relay succeeded X.25 and was designed for speed over more reliable networks. In application, we used it as a one technology to interconnect LANs. It was a packet switched technology, and it was developed because of higher data rates and lower error rates in 1990s high speed (!) communications systems. Information was sent in variable length packets (frames) through a shared frame relay network. Each frame contained all the information necessary to route it to the correct destination. Each Data Termination Equipment (DTE) endpoint could communicate with many destinations over one access link to the network.

Fig 3. Packet Switched Networks.

Some new concepts were introduced; Switched Virtual Circuits (SVCs) were temporary connections used in situations requiring only sporadic data transfer between DTE devices across the Frame Relay network. Permanent Virtual Circuits (PVCs) established connections that were used for frequent and consistent data transfers between DTE devices across the network. Communication across a PVC did not require the call setup and termination states that were used with SVCs.

Quality of service was also engineered into this solution. Frame Relay offered a Committed Information Rate (CIR) at which data could definitely be transmitted. If traffic and the SLA allow, then data could burst above the CIR to an Extended Information Rate (EIR). These frames were marked discard eligible (DE). Frames in excess of EIR were immediately dropped.

docs.title: 7. Cell Switched Networks
docs.text: These were a variation on circuit switched networks, where fixed sized packets (=cells) are transmitted as rapidly and simply as possible (e.g. unreliable) across virtual circuits. A typical technology was asynchronous transfer mode (ATM).

docs.title: Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM)
docs.text:
A successor was required to ISDN with higher bandwidth and with capabilities making it suitable for LAN extension and supporting video. The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) defined Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) as the vehicle for Broadband ISDN with a view to it becoming the universal network transport. Different from TDM, time slots were available on demand with information identifying the source of the transmission contained in the header of each ATM cell.

It mitigated all the known problems with protocols like Frame Relay and Ethernet and during the 1990s, it appeared that it would be become the emergent protocol. However, with the development of gigabit Ethernet, the industry fixed the underlying problems of latency and quality of service by throwing enormous bandwidth at the problem. That, as well as the economies of scale of Ethernet led to the eventual decline of ATM.

ATM was complex to engineer, especially in the LAN where various emulations were used. In used SVCs and PVCs and four quality of service rates were introduced, making traffic management very effective.

docs.title: 8. Point to Point
docs.text:
If you have a DSL circuit at home, you may still use some of this technology!

Point-to-point protocol (PPP) was intended to establish a direct link between two nodes on a point-to-point link. It allowed for multiple protocols. It supported authentication with Password Authentication Protocol (PAP) or Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP). It also had error detection, encryption, and compression. It was commonly used by ISPs for connections over Ethernet (PPoE) or ATM (PPoA). When setting up dial-up circuits over ISDN, this was used with indication. The stack model is shown in Fig 4.

Fig 4. The PtP Stack.

For encapsulation, it used High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC). To establish, configure, and test the data link connection, it used Link Control Protocol (LCP). PPP was designed to allow the simultaneous use of multiple network layer protocols and Network Control Protocol (NCP) was used for establishing and configuring these different network layer protocols.

Legacy communications equipment used modems, and at the router, a typical configuration is shown in Fig 5.

Fig 5. A PtP Configuration.

In the late 1900s, we would have taught data communications using serial ports. They have been dropped by most educators now. Its a pity, as you will still come across this technology in Military, Aerospace, Oil and Gas, etc.

Point to Point Protocol over Ethernet (PPP0E) encapsulates PPP packets in Ethernet frames. This technology is still used by ISPs for DSL termination. It is very suited for unbundled services to DSLAMs. It adds 8-byte overhead per packet, which can be very significant for small packets.
